historical_timeline.summary: Polio at age six, leaving the right leg thinner and shorter.
Bus struck by a streetcar: pelvic, spinal, collarbone, rib, and right leg fractures.
Began to paint while immobilized in bed.
Chronic pain, many operations, and about 25 corsets.
Stopped attending her classes at La Esmeralda because of limited mobility.
Nearly a year in hospital with an infection after a spinal graft.
Right leg amputated below the knee for threatened gangrene.
Died at the Blue House, aged 47.

claims.statement: Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo Calderón was born on July 6, 1907, in her parents' house in Coyoacán, Mexico City, now known as the Blue House, the daughter of Guillermo Kahlo and Matilde Calderón.
Frida Kahlo died at the Blue House in Mexico City on July 13, 1954, at the age of 47.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: In 1913, at the age of six, Kahlo fell ill with polio; afterward her right leg was thinner, slightly shorter, and less developed, with the foot turned outward, and her father encouraged cycling and swimming.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The contemporaneous diagnosis was polio; a retrospective analysis adds a congenital spinal anomaly.

claims.statement: A neurologist's retrospective review proposes that Kahlo also had a congenital spinal anomaly (spina bifida).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; kept off the active problem list.

claims.statement: On September 17, 1925, at 18, Kahlo was riding a bus that was struck by a streetcar; a metal handrail impaled her through the hip and fractured her pelvis, and she had three fractures of the spinal column, a fractured collarbone, two rib fractures, a dislocated right shoulder, and eleven fractures of the right leg with a dislocated foot.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented injuries behind the synthetic chronic pain diagnoses; stated without graphic detail.

source_links.locator: Abstract: a horrific trolley car accident in her teens

claims.statement: While immobilized for several months after the accident, Kahlo began to paint, using an easel adapted for painting in bed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A documented strength: art as a way through prolonged pain and bed rest.

claims.statement: Kahlo lived with chronic pain for the rest of her life, underwent many operations, some with long convalescences and serious consequences, and used about 25 different corsets.

source_links.locator: Abstract: lifelong chronic pain and numerous failed spinal surgeries

claims.statement: In 1944, because of increasingly limited mobility, Kahlo had to stop attending her classes at the La Esmeralda school of painting and sculpture, and some students continued to work with her at the Blue House.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented functional decline that anchors the index age.

claims.statement: Her pain has been interpreted retrospectively as including chronic neuropathic pain and central sensitization.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Modern pain-science interpretation; informs the synthetic multimodal plan.

claims.statement: In 1950 Kahlo spent nearly the whole year in hospital with an infection after a graft to her spinal column.
In 1953 Kahlo's right leg was amputated below the knee because of the threat of gangrene.
Kahlo's father, Guillermo Kahlo, had epilepsy and died in 1941; her mother, Matilde Calderón, died in 1932.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The cited source does not give causes of death.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Kahlo returns two weeks after her first visit, on the day of her physical medicine and rehabilitation consultation. The rehabilitation plan starts physical therapy twice a week with graded exercise, core and hip strengthening, and aquatic therapy, with a shoe lift for her shorter right leg; her first session is today. She has taken duloxetine 30 mg daily for two weeks. It caused mild nausea for the first few days, which has passed, and no dizziness, sweating, or sleep change. She takes acetaminophen 1 g three times a day and uses the diclofenac gel on her ankle, which makes standing easier. She still takes no more than four oxycodone tablets a day and has needed no early refills. The burning in her right leg is a little less at night. She can stand at the easel for about 15 minutes before the pain makes her sit. She has agreed to a first small reduction in her oxycodone dose at the four-week visit, provided her function holds, and asks that the taper stay slow.

She has gone to physical therapy twice a week, missing one aquatic session while she was ill, and wears the new shoe lift. She is ready for the first dose reduction she agreed to two weeks ago, and she starts weekly cognitive behavioral therapy for chronic pain today.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Kahlo returns six weeks after her first visit and two weeks after her oxycodone was reduced to 52.5 MME a day. She has had no yawning, gooseflesh, stomach cramps, diarrhea, restlessness, or loss of sleep beyond her usual. Her pain has not worsened, and her PEG is 5.3, 27 percent below the 7.3 she scored at intake. With the shoe lift she now stands at the easel for 25 to 30 minutes at a time. She goes to physical therapy twice a week and to cognitive behavioral therapy weekly, and she has had no falls. She takes acetaminophen 1 g three times a day. She asks when the next reduction will be and wants it to stay slow.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Kahlo is a 37-year-old woman with chronic post-traumatic back, pelvic, and right leg pain on long-term oxycodone (60 MME a day), who asked for a same-day visit. Her duloxetine was increased to 60 mg a week ago at the rehabilitation visit, and she takes acetaminophen 1 g three times a day. Three days ago she developed a scratchy throat, then a clear runny nose, congestion, and a dry cough. Several of the students who come to her studio have had colds. Home COVID-19 antigen tests on the first and third days were negative. Her highest home temperature was 37.8 °C. Coughing fits jolt her lower back and pelvis, and the pain is worse at night, but she has kept to no more than four oxycodone tablets a day. She bought a nighttime cold and flu liquid at the pharmacy and brought it unopened to ask whether it is safe. Its label lists acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, and doxylamine. She missed one aquatic therapy session. Her oxycodone dose has not changed, and she has had no yawning, gooseflesh, stomach cramps, diarrhea, or restlessness.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Kahlo returns for an adult preventive visit, booked separately from her pain care. The cold she had two weeks ago cleared within ten days without antibiotics. One week ago her oxycodone was reduced from 60 to 52.5 MME a day, and she reports no withdrawal symptoms and pain she can manage, with a PEG of 5.7 today. She attends physical therapy twice a week and cognitive behavioral therapy weekly, and she has had no falls since starting care here. She received this season's influenza vaccine last week. She does not recall when she last had cervical cancer screening, and no result is on record. She explains that lying on an examination table with her legs raised aggravates her back and hip pain, so she would prefer to avoid a speculum examination if she can. She completed the health risk assessment before the visit.

referral.question: Chronic post-traumatic back, pelvic, and right leg pain after old spinal and pelvic fractures, spinal surgery, and childhood polio, in a 37-year-old painter on long-term opioid therapy. Please design a multimodal rehabilitation plan, review bracing and orthotics, including a shoe lift for her leg-length difference, and set function goals that can guide a slow opioid taper
referral.pertinent_history: Constant low back and pelvic pain with burning in the right leg. It limits how long she can stand at the easel, and she has had to stop teaching at the art school; some students now come to her studio. She walks short distances with a cane and a limp from the shorter, weaker right leg, uses a wheelchair for longer outings, and wears a back brace on bad days. Today's right ankle radiograph shows post-traumatic osteoarthritis, with joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, and healed old fractures. Oxycodone 10 mg up to four times a day (60 MME) for about two and a half years from another prescriber; a single prescriber on the monitoring program and a urine drug test consistent with oxycodone only. She fears a sudden cut in her dose, and any taper will be slow and agreed with her. PEG 7.3; PHQ-9 8 with no thoughts of self-harm; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 18 ng/mL. Started today: duloxetine 30 mg, scheduled acetaminophen, diclofenac gel for the ankle, vitamin D, and naloxone
questions: What exercise and physical therapy program best fits her spine, pelvis, polio-affected leg, and ankle?
Would a shoe lift, ankle bracing, or a change in how she uses her back brace help?
Do any findings call for imaging, nerve testing, or an interventional procedure?
What function goals should we use to judge progress as the opioid dose is slowly reduced?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Kahlo is seen at the request of Dr. Ortega for chronic post-traumatic pain. She describes constant low back and pelvic pain with burning in the right leg, a little less at night since she started duloxetine two weeks ago, and right ankle pain on standing that the diclofenac gel eases. She can stand at the easel for about 15 minutes before she has to sit, and she paints mostly seated or reclining. She walks short distances with a cane, uses a wheelchair for longer outings, and wears her back brace on bad days. She has had no falls, no new weakness or numbness, and no change in bladder or bowel control. She takes no more than four oxycodone tablets a day. She knows a slow opioid taper is planned and asks that it stay slow. Her own goals are to stand longer at the easel and to keep teaching and painting every day
